title: Introduction to R
text:
The aim of this practical is to get used to the R environment. The best way to do this is to start with something you already know about: basic statistics from your first and second year. Along the way we will introduce basic concepts common to all programming languages, with no prior programming knowledge assumed.






Learning objectives



By the end of this practical, you will be able to:

Use RStudio to write, comment, and execute lines of code.
Create and manipulate objects in R.
Load data files into R.
Calculate basic summary statistics.
Implement common inferential tests, including a t-test, correlation, and ANOVA.

title: Introduction to R
text:
2.1 Top left: Scripts
The top left quadrant is for your scripts. You won’t see this quadrant when you first open R, but it will appear when you create one in Section 3.
Scripts are like lists of instructions for the computer to follow. You can save them for future use, and this makes it easy to set up complex analyses without typing them in by hand each time or needing to click through multiple options.
Throughout these practicals, you will create several scripts that you can later adapt and reuse in running statistical analyses.

title: Introduction to R
text:
2.2 Bottom left: Console
The lower left window is called the Console. This is where the magic happens! Here, you can type in individual commands to ask the computer to do something. You can use it just like a calculator: try clicking in the console and typing 20 + 57 (or any other sum you choose!). If you press the Enter/Return key, the answer will print below.
We can also instruct the computer to create an “object” (or “variable”1). An object is like a box that you can store information in. Some objects are big, such as large datasets that contain many numbers or even chunks of text. Others might contain only one number.
Let’s create an object called a, and give it the value 5. Click on the Console area and type:

a <- 5

Then hit the Enter/Return key to run it. You will encounter the arrows <- a lot in R: they are used to assign (or store) everything on the right to the name that you provide on the left2.

title: Introduction to R
text:
2.3 Top right: Environment
If you have created an object, a, it should now appear in the top right section, in the Environment tab. This means that we can now treat a as though it is a number: we can run mathematical operations on the object, and get out an answer that depends on the value assigned. Try this now by typing a*2 into the console to multiply it by two, or a^2 to square it.
So why not just type 5^2 in the first place? Objects are useful because we can change and update their values, or include many numbers in them. Let’s make a new object called b with the numbers 1-5, and see what happens when we square it:

b <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
b^2

You should see that we now get a list of the squares of all the elements.
We will use objects to store and manipulate data in R, similar to how we might work on a spreadsheet or SPSS file. You can always inspect the objects you have to hand and the values assigned to them in the Environment panel.

title: Introduction to R
text:
2.4 Bottom right: Other things!
The bottom right window has several sections that can be navigated by clicking on the tabs at the top. Files shows the files in the directory that we are working from, Plots will contain any figures that we create, Packages contains a list of extensions that will enable us to do different types of statistics, and the Help table will show the help pages for a particular function if we ask for them (we’ll do this a lot!).

title: Introduction to R
text:
3.1 Opening your R Project
Make sure that you are working in the R Project ARM_Practicals. This should be the case if you have just completed the set-up instructions instructions. If not, or if you closed RStudio in between, you can open this by clicking File >> Open Project… and navigating to the project file we created.
Remember, it should say “ARM_Practicals” in the top-right corner of the RStudio window.



Current R Project open

title: Introduction to R
text:
3.2 Creating a script
You can create a new script by clicking File >> New File >> R Script, or using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+N.
Now you have a script open, let’s save it so that we can retain our work beyond today. Click File >> Save As… and navigate to the scripts folder inside the ARM_Practicals folder you created. Once you are in this folder, save your script with the name ARM1_intro.R.

title: Introduction to R
text:
3.3 Loading data into R
There is a file in the Practical Materials section of the VLE called ARM1_data1_gamers.csv. This is a .csv file, which is a readily used data storage format that can be opened in many different software3. Download this file, and save it in the folder we previously created (likely Documents/ARM_Practicals/data/).
At the top of your script file, you can now instruct R to read in the dataset by adding the following line:

gamer_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM1_data1_gamers.csv")

We are creating an object in R here called gamer_dat, and using the <- to assign something to it. Here, we want to assign the data file that we load in, so need to instruct it to find and load the data file. We use read.csv() to tell R that we want to load in a csv file. We tell it the file path to where the dataset is stored: the ./ affirms that we are starting in the current directory (your R project folder), then data/ instructs it to look in the data folder, then the final part is the name of the file (including the .csv extension).
Now you have typed this into your script, you need to execute it. You can do this by highlighting it with your mouse and then clicking ‘Run’ at the top of the script. Alternatively, if your cursor is on the correct line, you can hit Ctrl + Enter on your keyboard.
If you are successful, you should see an object called gamer_dat appear in the Environment tab. The information tells us it has 100 observations (rows) for 5 variables (columns). If you click the little grid to the right of this description, you can inspect the dataset in your top left panel. The five columns of the dataset correspond to:

ppt_id: a unique identifying code for each participant
age_years: their age in years
gamer: whether they play video games (y) or not (n)
hours: if they do play video games, how many hours they play per week on average (or NA if they don’t, meaning that it’s a missing value)
wmc: working memory capacity

This dataset was simulated for the purposes of today’s practical, but was inspired by a research study by Dr Fiona McNab.

title: Introduction to R
text:
5.1 Running a t-test
In Years 1 and 2, you learned about some inferential statistics that test the relationship between two variables.
Let’s test the hypothesis that gamers versus non-gamers have different working memory capacity in our dataset. We can use a t-test to analyse the difference in means between two groups. Add the following line of code to your script:

t.test(wmc ~ gamer, data = gamer_dat)

Within the t.test() call, we have asked for our dependent variable (wmc) to be predicted by (~) the variable gamer, which we know has two levels in the dataset (y, n). We don’t actually have objects called wmc and gamer in our R environment, so we need to specify that it should look for these within the gamer_dat dataset.
Execute the line of code. The output should reiterate the test you have run, and provide the necessary values for reporting on the third line of output: the t-statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value.
Is there a significant difference between the two groups (p < .05)? What is the mean working memory capacity for each group?

title: Introduction to R
text:
5.2 Running a correlation
Another simple analysis for testing the relationship between two variables is a correlation: the strength of association between two continuous variables. Let’s test how working memory capacity relates to age by typing and executing the following line.

cor.test(formula = ~ age_years + wmc, data = gamer_dat)

Again, the output should tell you the test that has been done. Does the p-value show that there’s a significant relationship between the two? The final line of output (labelled “cor”) is the correlation coefficient. What happens to working memory as age increases?
::: {.callout-tip title-“Getting help with functions”=““} These calls for statistical tests that we have just run are called functions. We also used functions above to read in the data, and gain some summary statistics. You can find out more about the options available for each function by typing e.g., help(t.test) or help(cor.test) in the Console (this is a bit meta, we use the help() function to ask for help about other functions). This should bring up some helpful information in the bottom right window.
The help pages tell you which “Arguments” you need to give to the function, and how to specify them. For example, we can see that to run a Spearman test rather than a Pearson’s correlation, we should add the argument method = "spearman" inside the brackets. Try this now. :::

title: Introduction to R
text:
5.3 Running an ANOVA
Finally, let’s r a simple one-way ANOVA. Now you’ve established that gamers have a higher working memory capacity than non-gamers, we might want to ask whether it matters what type of games people are playing. You run a new study and recruit only young adults who self-report as gamers. You measure their working capacity, and ask them to select their dominant game type.
Make sure that you have downloaded the data from the VLE and saved it in your data folder. Load it into R and assign it to an object called type_dat. Inspect the dataset to see the game categories.

type_dat <- read.csv("./data/ARM1_data2_gametype.csv")

Given there are three levels of game type, we can no longer use a t-test to compare working memory between groups. Instead, we can use a one-way ANOVA.
The first step in running an ANOVA is to check the assumption of homogeneity of variance using Levene’s test. This test isn’t included as standard in R, so we need to load in a package (a set of functions that someone has written) to run it. You only need to run this once in each R session. Add the following lines to your script5, and run them:

# Load car package
library(car)

# Run Levene's test
leveneTest(wmc ~ type, data = type_dat)

The output first prints a warning that it interpreted our group (i.e., game type) as a factor. This is fine, that’s what we want it to do! You should then see that the test is not significant (p > .05), so we can assume that the variances are equal across the groups. This means we can proceed with our ANOVA.
We can run the test and display the results using only two lines of code:

# Run ANOVA and save output to object
gametype_model <- aov(wmc ~ type, data = type_dat)

# Print output summary
summary(gametype_model)

This will produce your ANOVA summary table as follows:


            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
type         2  70.42   35.21   11.12 5.01e-05 ***
Residuals   87 275.53    3.17                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Just like in SPSS, we can pick out the degrees of freedom (2, 87), the F ratio (11.12) and the p-value (< .001). This tells us that there is a significant difference in working memory capacity depending on the type of game that people play most regularly.






Why does my p-value look weird?





When numbers get very small, R defaults to scientific notation. Perhaps some of you are experienced in reading this, but I am not. If you want to turn this off, add options(scipen=999) to the top of your scripts.

title: Introduction to R
text:
6.1 Challenge yourself
If you have completed the practical in good time and want to challenge yourself, have a go at the following independent exercise. Use the first dataset (ARM1_data1_gamers.csv) to look more closely at the number of hours played.

Use the descriptive statistics functions to work out the mean and standard deviation of this variable.
Find one or more functions that give us the minimum and maximum number of hours played in the dataset.
Examine the correlation between working memory capacity and the number of hours played, for the gamers only.

You are very likely to encounter some errors along the way, and there are multiple ways to solve the problem! Try using the R help files or googling to find a solution for yourself: this is a major part of coding! Check back here to see solution(s) after the practical.

title: Introduction to R
text:
6.2 Further learning
You do not need to become an expert in R to do well in this module, but it’s one way of getting to grips with different statistical techniques and many students enjoy the challenge. If you’re serious about learning R, then the following DataCamp chapters are relevant to this week’s content and will help to consolidate the material ready for the practicals ahead. You will need to sign up for a free account using the link from the VLE Module Information page.

Introduction to R
Hypothesis Testing in R

You might also be interested in the R version of the Andy Field textbook (Discovering Statistics using R), if this is a familiar learning style for you. It has many example data sets and details of how to do different tests, and there are plenty of copies available in the library. Alternatively, there is a fantastic textbook for undergraduate psychology students developed by Danielle Navarro, which you can access for free online.







How’s it going?



Let us know how today went via this quick survey via this survey - rate the difficulty and length, and leave any comments that would help for us to know (positive comments welcome too!). You will need to be logged in with your university account to respond, but your submission will be anonymous.
For more general questions about the practical, please post them on the VLE Discussion Board.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Footnotes


In programming, “variables” are used to store information in memory. In R, a language used for statistics, these are commonly referred to as “objects” to avoid confusion with the use of “variable” in relation to your data (i.e., a column in your dataset, your independent/dependent variables). You will see these referred to as either, and either is fine.↩︎
If you already have some programming experience, you might be more used to using the = symbol to assign values. This works fine in R too so can be used if you prefer. However, using the <- is more clearly distinguished from other aspects of R code, and so is more readily used/taught.↩︎
If you wish to read in different file types in the future (e.g., .xlsx, .sav), there are many different bespoke packages available that will support you in doing this (e.g., read_excel, haven).↩︎
The eagle-eyed among you might also see that you have your first example of rainbow brackets, if you turned on this setting during the set-up task!↩︎
University machines have this package ready installed. If you are using your own machine, you will need to install the car package first. You can do this by running install.packages("car").You only need to do this once, so can type it directly into the console.↩︎

title: Getting set up for the module
text: You should complete these brief set-up steps first before you begin the practical sessions, and any time you begin working on a new device (e.g., if you swap between a university machine and your laptop).

title: Getting set up for the module
text:
3.1 Set up your folders
Let’s first create a folder to store all of your practical work.

Open the file browser on your computer. On Windows, you can do this by clicking Start >> File Explorer.
Navigate to your Documents folder.
Create a new folder, and call it “ARM_Practicals”.
Within this new folder, create one folder called “scripts”, and another folder called “data”.







Tip



R is case-sensitive, meaning that if you capitalise letters here then you will also need to be specific in your capitalisation in the scripts. It is a good idea to adopt a consistent approach to avoid later issues. Here we have used lower case, and strongly advise you to do the same so that you don’t get confused later on.


When you download datasets for the practicals in the future, you should save them in your data folder. Similarly, when you create scripts in each practical, save them in the scripts folder.

title: Getting set up for the module
text:
3.2 Initiate an R Project
Now let’s tell R where we want to work during these practicals.

Open RStudio.
At the top of the window, click File >> New Project…
After a bit of thinking (be patient!), a “New Project Wizard” window should appear. Click the Existing Directory option in the middle, to associate this new project with an existing working directory. We choose this option because we have already set up our folder in the previous step.
On the next window, click “Browse…” and then navigate to your ARM_Practicals folder. Once you are in it (and can see your data/scripts folders), click “Open”.
Click “Create Project”.

The name of the R Project you are working in should now show in the top right hand corner of your window.



The current R Project


If it doesn’t, retrace your steps and try again. If it still doesn’t work, put your hand up and ask for help.

title: Getting set up for the module
text:
3.3 Moving forwards
The instructions for the practicals will assume that you have set up R in this way. We will follow three key principles:

Open the R Project at the start of every session. You can do this by double clicking it from your file browser, or clicking File >> Open Project… from within RStudio.
Save the data files in the data folder, once you have downloaded them from the VLE.
Save your scripts in the scripts folder.

More on what these mean in the remainder of Practical 1!

title: Getting set up for the module
text:
4.1 Saving the workspace
An irritating default of RStudio is that it saves everything automatically on exiting. This might sound like a great idea, but in reality it can mean that you have a very messy workspace and that mistakes emerge from using old material. It is highly recommended that you turn this off by taking the following steps:

At the top of RStudio, click Tools >> Global Options…
On the General panel that should open in the window, there is a section titled Workspace.
Make sure that the Restore .RData[…] box is unticked, and that it is set to never save the workspace on exit.
Click “Apply” to save the settings.




Global options window with recommended General settings

title: Getting set up for the module
text:
4.2 Rainbow parentheses
Sometimes we will need to wrap things inside multiple nested brackets. You don’t need to worry about what this means for now, but while we’re on the settings, we can set up one of my favourite RStudio features: rainbow parentheses! This setting colour codes your brackets so that you can tell which ones are paired together. And who doesn’t want a bit of colour on their scripts?!

On the Global Options… window you have open, click on “Code” down the left hand side.
Click the “Display” tab at the top.
Under syntax, check the box that says “Use rainbow parentheses”.
Then click “Apply”, and/or “OK” to close the window.




Global options window with recommended Code Display settings


As for what this has done? Well, you’ll just have to wait and see as we get writing scripts…

title: 1 Introduction to the module
text:
Welcome to Advanced Research Methods!
Each week’s lecture content is available via the VLE module page. These course pages are where you will find the materials for the practical sessions. Each practical session will have its own page of instructions released throughout the semester. Instructions can also be downloaded in Word or PDF format should you prefer: find the links underneath the outline down the lefthand side of each page.
This page outlines how to approach the practical sessions. Before you begin in Week 1—and anytime you switch devices—you should also check out the guidelines for setting up your workspace for this module.

title: 1 Introduction to the module
text:
2.1 Preparation
We expect that you will come to this session having attended the lecture on Tuesday, or caught up via the recording if you were unable to make it in person. We also recommend that you should have done the core reading for the week to consolidate your understanding. Having done so will help you to engage fully with the practical session, and also enable you to ask questions about aspects that you did not understand.

title: 1 Introduction to the module
text:
2.2 During the practical
The practical is self-paced. You should work through the instructions to create and annotate your own analysis script, checking your understanding and taking notes as you go.
Where we have hidden code sections, do your best to try and figure out the solution yourself before peeking! Trial and error is a much more effective way of learning, and will help you to build your coding skills.
You can count on getting stuck at various points during the practical sessions. Errors are a very normal part of coding, even if sometimes frustrating! If you get stuck, try the following:

Spend time trying some different things! What’s happening that you don’t expect? Is there an error message, and does it tell you anything useful?
Google it! Copying and pasting the error message into Google often takes you to help forums where others have asked about the same problem.
Chat to the person next to you—maybe they can spot something in your code that you can’t see?
Put your hand up, and we’ll come over to help!




Artwork by @allison_horst


While it’s a good idea to spend a bit time trying to tackle a problem yourself, do keep in mind the long-term goals of the practical. Don’t struggle on Step 1 for 50 minutes and run out of time for the rest! We’re here to help you make progress.
